policy: Every dataset entry is either generated in this repository (origin 'generated-in-repo') or imported from an external source with a license and an immutable pin. An import without both is rejected by the integrity suite.

sources.note: Synthetic version-range records. They are not real advisories and are never counted toward the real-advisory minimum.

nistSard.note: NIST SARD is not known to provide Haskell or Nix/NixOS cases. No SARD or Juliet case is used or claimed for either ecosystem.

gaps.requirement: at least 10 real pinned HSEC/upstream advisory records
gaps.reason: needs network access to the advisory database; no record is fabricated to fill the count

gaps.requirement: at least 3 pinned Haskell canary projects
gaps.reason: needs network access to fetch and pin upstream commits and licenses

gaps.requirement: at least 3 pinned Nix/NixOS canary configurations
gaps.reason: needs network access to fetch and pin upstream commits and licenses
ghc, cabal and nix are not installed in the build environment; fixtures are reviewed by the independent label reviewer only, not compiled or evaluated

changed: haskell/privacy-lineage (sinks use imported, real APIs; field ipAddr renamed ipAddress to match the taxonomy)
revisions.reason: Label-validity defects found while measuring on the development splits, not detector tuning: the v1 route-authentication "guard" was a no-op stub (`requireAuth = pure ()`), which is not authentication, and its handlers performed no state change; the v1 object-authorization cases were plain functions that ignored a parameter, not request handlers with an id lookup. A safe label on a stub guard and a vulnerable label on a handler with no sensitive operation are not defensible labels. v2 uses a credential-reading guard that rejects with 401 and handlers that persist a change, in both labels. The route-authentication handlers were later changed again, before any holdout was ever scored, to operations with no object id (a cache purge, a settings update): the id-keyed delete they used also had a latent object-authorization defect that appears once the route is authenticated, so a "safe" route-authentication case carried a second defect.
revisions.oldFailuresRecorded: v1 holdout results for these two families are not published as a measurement; the v1 corpus is preserved in git history.
revisions.holdoutRule: Only the holdout cases of the listed families changed; every other holdout hash is identical to v1. None of the changed holdout cases was used to tune a detector.
revisions.nixReason: Same class of label-validity defect, found on the development splits: configurations where the service is not enabled (sshd, postgresql, nginx, doas, a systemd unit with no ExecStart/wantedBy), whose options are inert on NixOS; a "safe" ssh configuration that left PasswordAuthentication at its NixOS default (true); a "least-capability" service that still ran as root; a TLS "vulnerable" shape that used a /etc/ssl/private string path (a runtime path, not a defect) in place of a Nix path literal (copied into the store); and two shapes with attribute syntax that is not valid Nix (`systemd.services.${appName}-job`). Detector behaviour was not the reason for any of these edits. The dangerous-capability service shape also named no User, so the service ran as root as well as holding the capability (two defects in one case, against a one-defect-per-case design); it now names a non-root User. The root-login shape left PasswordAuthentication at its NixOS default (true), so it carried a second defect; it now disables password authentication so each vulnerable case seeds one defect.
revisions.privacyReason: The v1 Haskell privacy sources named functions that were never imported and one invented API (`postJson`), used an undefined `maskTail`, and unparenthesised accessor applications (`hashWith SHA256 email acct`); the sinks now use real imported APIs and the protections are well-formed. No holdout field changed split (the holdout fields are still ssn, address, passport).
